issues.legal_issue: A lease granted by an agent without the authority required by the principal is invalid.
material_facts: The disputed properties were leased by the principal’s agent to the original lessee, rather than by the principal himself.
The agent’s written authority prohibited leasing the properties without the principal’s or his manager’s written consent.
No written consent was produced, and the appellate revenue authority found that the principal had not consented.
issues.conclusion: The lease in favour of the appellants was invalid because the agent lacked authority to grant it.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the terms of the agent’s written authority: because the authority required written consent before the properties could be leased, a lease granted without that consent was invalid. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.tenancy_possession_suit: A claimant brought a tenancy proceeding seeking possession of property held by another person.
predicates.agent_lease_requires_consent: The principal’s agent was permitted to lease the property only if the principal or an authorised manager consented.
predicates.consent_not_given: The required consent was not given before the agent granted the lease.

issues.definition: When a tenancy possession suit concerns a lease granted by an agent who required consent, and that consent was not given, the agent granted the lease without the required authority.

issues.legal_issue: A contention that was not raised before the revenue tribunal cannot be considered for the first time in a writ challenge to its decision.
material_facts: In the writ petition, the appellants argued that the principal had subsequently ratified the lease granted by the agent.
The Letters Patent Bench found that the ratification contention had not been urged before the Board of Revenue.
The Supreme Court held that the single Judge should not have considered that contention.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to consider the ratification contention because it had not been raised before the Board of Revenue.
issues.legal_principle: In reviewing a tribunal’s decision under Article 226, the High Court should not consider a contention that was not advanced before that tribunal. No earlier case was relied on for this proposition.

predicates.certiorari_writ: A party sought a writ challenging a tribunal’s decision.
predicates.plea_not_raised_before_tribunal: The party did not advance the contention before the tribunal whose decision was challenged.

issues.definition: In a writ challenging a tribunal’s decision, a contention not raised before that tribunal cannot be considered by the High Court.

issues.legal_issue: A possession suit is not barred by limitation when the affirmed finding is that the defendants began possession only recently enough for the suit to be timely.
material_facts: The Additional Commissioner found that the appellants took possession of the properties only in 1950.
The Board of Revenue treated that finding as a finding of fact binding on it and agreed with the Additional Commissioner’s conclusions.
The appellants’ contention that inadmissible evidence supported the possession finding had not been raised before the Board of Revenue.
The Supreme Court found ample evidence supporting the possession finding and held that, on that finding, the suit was within time.
issues.conclusion: The suit was within time and was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: The court accepted the affirmed factual finding about when possession began and concluded that the suit was timely on that basis. It also held that the High Court should not entertain an evidentiary objection that had not been raised before the Board of Revenue. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

rule.if: tenancy_possession_suit and possession_began_recently_enough_for_suit and possession_finding_supported_by_evidence and evidence_objection_not_raised_before_tribunal

predicates.tenancy_possession_suit: A claimant brought a tenancy proceeding seeking possession of property held by another person.
predicates.possession_began_recently_enough_for_sui: The defendants’ possession began only recently enough that the possession finding made the claimant’s suit timely.
predicates.possession_finding_supported_by_evidence: The finding about when possession began was supported by evidence.
predicates.evidence_objection_not_raised_before_tri: The party challenging the evidence did not raise that objection before the tribunal whose decision was challenged.

issues.definition: A tenancy possession suit is not barred by limitation when the supported finding is that possession began recently enough for the suit to be timely and the evidentiary objection was not raised before the tribunal.

issues.legal_issue: Certiorari jurisdiction cannot be exercised merely because a question of law could be raised; the challenged order must suffer from an error of law apparent on the face of the record.
material_facts: The single Judge remanded the matter because questions of law could be urged on the material before the court.
The single Judge did not find that the Board of Revenue’s order was vitiated by an error of law apparent on the face of the record.
The Letters Patent Bench reversed the single Judge, and the Supreme Court held that the single Judge’s approach was untenable.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not quash the Board of Revenue’s order on the basis of the mere possibility of raising questions of law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, the High Court may use certiorari to quash an order for an error of law only when the order suffers from an error of law apparent on the face of the record; the mere possibility of raising a question of law is insufficient. No earlier case was cited.

predicates.certiorari_writ: A party sought certiorari review of a tribunal’s order.
predicates.challenged_order_lacks_apparent_error_of: The reviewing court did not find an error of law apparent on the face of the challenged order.
predicates.only_possible_legal_question_identified: The reviewing court identified only a question of law that might be argued, without finding an apparent legal error in the order.

issues.definition: In certiorari review, if no apparent error of law is found and only a possible legal question is identified, certiorari cannot issue on that basis alone.
